doc.title: Michael White interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 10, 2025

title: Music schools and Juilliard coaching
summary: White says teaching the music requires respecting it, hates the corny Dixieland image, and describes coaching Juilliard bands playing King Oliver and Jelly Roll Morton before Covid.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: I try not to think about chords initially. I try to think about sound and phrases. Melodic phrases. And then after I go for a while then I’m let’s see now, how many bars is this, what are the chords. And I might start to put chords on top of it or might not initially. I might wait to the end and try to figure out what they are. But I don’t want to be too constricted by structure and traditional structure. I want to kind of hear my own thing sometimes. Sometimes I use conventional structures very easily, like the blues. So if I hear a windshield wiper that, you know I was at the red light the other day [claps rhythm]. And sometimes the movement is the backbeat. So you hear that you know, and that might imply something like [plays clarinet]. You know, something like that. And then I’ll take off on the melody from there. But the rhythm is what inspires those melodies. So I think rhythm is extremely important in that sense. You know, but in terms of, I wanted to finish that thing out about the music schools, two things. One is in order to teach that music, the first thing you have to do is respect it. You have to understand that this is a valid art form, it’s as valid as bebop or post-bebop or any other form of jazz. And it has certain musical principles. The problem is that people don’t know the history and they think it’s just this comic, fast, straw hat, Dixieland stuff and that’s kind of like wrong. You know that exists and that’s kind of like some kind of offshoot and all of that, but that’s not what this music is. It’s not what it’s about. But you see it commercialized that way many times, and people, you know, “New Orleans jazz, oh this” you know and they expect you to be you know goofy acting and playing all kind of corny stuff and all that. I hate that stuff I really do. That’s not what I play. That’s not the tradition I come from. So the other thing is in terms of music schools, Juilliard in recent years has been

pioneering in the fact that they’ve included early New Orleans jazz as part of their repertoire, and for several years before Covid I was a guest coach and I would go in and coach several bands that had the charge of playing the music of let’s say King Oliver or Jelly Roll Morton, and what they would do is they would have to transcribe the song. Everybody had to transcribe all the parts and then they would put it together and then they would all, you know, play the songs, and I would go in and talk about the tempo, the volume, the feeling, what was going on with the rhythm, things like that. And I really loved it, and it was great to hear them seriously approaching the music without feeling that they had to put bebop in it. They didn’t sound like bebop players. You know? So I’d go to a concert with them, you know, playing King Oliver, the next night they’re playing Charles Lloyd or something and they sound like that, you know, so that was amazing to me. But what that does is, and then there are a lot of other players I think influenced by YouTube that don’t think that you know the older modern jazz is the only way to go in playing jazz. So I like people who are experimenting in different styles. Guys that experiment in the more modern styles I like that but also experimenting in traditional styles. Because you know I write songs every day that are different. And they are influenced by a wide range of things. You mentioned “Give It Up” – the song I wrote “Give It Up” which has evolved now to include a big drum solo and a clarinet and drum duet. But that song, which some people say sounds like klezmer to them originally was influenced by a Jabbo Smith song. I heard that and I was thinking about the structure and that’s what I was coming at. You know? But I wanted to write songs that have catchy, simple melodies that people could relate to after the band stops playing, that the next day they’re humming that melody.
